name: Netherlands
tagline: Hundreds of English-taught degrees, and a system that is changing
ownCitizens: If you hold Dutch citizenship, the parts of this page written for other EU/EEA citizens — registering your right of residence, proving your fee status — are not about you, and the Netherlands' own student grants and loans are open to you on their ordinary terms; check them, because some depend on where you have lived. Your IB is still a foreign qualification here, so the IB entry rules on this page still apply to you.
summary: The Netherlands is a common choice for an IB student in Denmark who wants an English-taught degree in Europe: hundreds of bachelor programmes taught entirely in English, three-year research-university degrees, a low statutory fee, and an application process that runs through one portal. All of that is still true and the first part of it is contracting, because a law now going through requires bachelor programmes to be taught mainly in Dutch unless the institution can justify otherwise. Universities have already begun converting and capping English tracks.
whyConsider: Hundreds of English-taught bachelor’s degrees, at both research universities and universities of applied sciences.
A full IB Diploma is compared by Nuffic to a VWO diploma, which is the qualification that opens a research university bachelor.
One portal, two deadlines, and a genuinely national process rather than institution-by-institution applications.
The statutory tuition fee is low by international standards and the same at every publicly funded institution.
watchOuts: The internationalisation law is the thing to watch. Check in autumn 2026 that the specific programme you want will still be taught in English in September 2027 — not that the university still offers English-taught programmes, but that yours does.

Numerus fixus is not a formality. You may apply to at most two selective programmes in a year, and medicine, dentistry, dental hygiene and physiotherapy allow only one application per programme, so you cannot apply for medicine at two universities. That is a real constraint on strategy and it is decided in January.

"15 January or 1 May" is not the whole story, and believing it will cost you a place. Of the sixteen programmes now recorded here, the Dutch numerus fixus ones close on 15 January; University College Maastricht closes on 1 April for an EU applicant and 1 February for everyone else; Breda's selective programmes close in Studielink on 1 May but want a portfolio from the previous November; Erasmus wants its own form by 31 January, a fortnight after Studielink; and Twente closed a day early, on 30 April. Read the programme page, not the country page, for the date that binds you.

Studielink does not require a DigiD if you live outside the Netherlands: you create an account by uploading a scan or photo of your passport or EU identity card, which is verified automatically. Do it well before 15 January.
Housing in the university cities is severe. Several institutions warn applicants not to arrive without a confirmed room.
There is no national IB-to-Dutch grade conversion. If you are coming from the Danish system, do not go looking for one.

Several Dutch selections score the grades of your penultimate school year — your DP1 results — and say outright that predicted grades are not used. Rotterdam School of Management and Maastricht both do this. If you are reading this in DP1, those are the grades that will decide it.

ibRecognition.minimumPoints: A full IB Diploma requires 24 points, and that is the floor rather than a target: individual programmes and numerus fixus selection routinely expect considerably more. Nuffic publishes no national minimum score, and there is no national IB-to-Dutch conversion table at all — the conversionTable field is deliberately absent rather than unfilled.
ibRecognition.subjectLevelRule: Nuffic compares the full IB Diploma to a Dutch VWO diploma, the qualification that gives access to a research university bachelor. Programmes requiring specific subjects — mathematics and physics for engineering, mathematics for economics and econometrics — normally want them at Higher Level, and each university publishes its own list. Check the programme page rather than a national rule, because there is not one.

language.englishTaughtBachelors: Extensive by European standards and contracting. The count published today may not hold for 2027 entry.
language.englishProof: Set per programme, not nationally. IB English A or English B at Higher Level is commonly accepted, and many programmes waive a test for anyone who completed an entirely English-taught secondary education such as the IB. Confirm on the programme page.
notes: Dutch is not required for an English-taught programme, and is worth some effort anyway: the housing market, part-time work and student life all open up with it.

feeContext.summary: The statutory fee (wettelijk collegegeld), the same at every publicly funded institution. €2,694 for 2026–27; the 2027–28 figure is set annually by government and is not yet published.
The institutional fee, set by each institution and substantially higher than the statutory rate. Not established here for 2027–28; check the institution directly.

sectorLandscape.summary: The Netherlands divides higher education in two, and the division matters more than almost anything else a student will read about the country. Research universities (universiteit, WO) and universities of applied sciences (hogeschool, HBO) are parallel systems with different entry qualifications, different lengths, and different purposes — not a ranking. An IB Diploma opens both. Most English-language advice describes only the first.

routes.what: The WO route. A three-year bachelor followed by a one- or two-year master, academic in emphasis and taught by researchers. This is what an IB Diploma is compared to in Dutch terms, and what nearly all English-language guidance is describing.

The HBO route. Four years rather than three, including a substantial placement and often a second one, and built around doing the work rather than studying the discipline. Strong in engineering, business, hotel and event management, design, health and teaching. An IB Diploma is more than sufficient for entry, and Dutch students reach it from HAVO — one level below the VWO an IB compares to.
routes.note: Habitually described as the lesser option, which misreads it. It is the more vocational option, and for a student who wants to be employable in the subject rather than continue to a master, it is frequently the better one.

routes.what: Small selective honours colleges attached to research universities — Amsterdam, Utrecht, Leiden, Maastricht and others. Broad liberal-arts first year narrowing later, taught in English, usually residential, and closer to a US liberal-arts college than anything else in Europe. They select on more than grades and they charge more than the statutory fee.
routes.note: Often a strong fit for an IB student, precisely because the breadth-then-depth structure resembles the Diploma.

routes.what: Art, design, music, dance and theatre, admitting on portfolio or audition. Grades are secondary and the entry process runs on a different calendar and different terms from everything else here.
routes.note: Not researched in detail here. Recorded because it exists and because a student who needs it will not find it in the ordinary listings.

notes: Re-check in autumn 2026: the statutory fee for 2027–28 (not published by DUO on 2026-09-24), and whether the internationalisation law has passed. On 2026-09-24 bill 36555 was still at committee stage in the Tweede Kamer.
Resolved 2026-09-24: an applicant without a DigiD creates a Studielink account by uploading an ID scan (ev-studielink-no-digid).

THE NETHERLANDS NEEDS NO RECOGNITION SCHEME, and data/recognition/nl.json is deliberately absent. This was the question ADR 0002 left open and it is now answered from sixteen Opportunities at five institutions rather than predicted. Nearly every Dutch entry requirement found in this pass is published in the IB's own vocabulary — named IB subjects at named IB levels, often with named IB grades. TU Delft: "Mathematics: AA HL + Physics HL". Maastricht: "International Business — Mathematics Analysis and Approaches SL/HL or Mathematics Applications and Interpretation SL/HL". Erasmus School of Economics: "English A HL (4) or English A SL (5) or English B HL (5)". There is nothing to translate and no local subject scale for these requirements to sit on. Nuffic, the recognition body, compares the IB Diploma to a VWO diploma at the level of the whole qualification and publishes no subject or grade conversion at all; ev-nuffic-ib-grades records that absence and why it is a finding rather than a gap.

The one real counter-example is recorded rather than smoothed away. University of Twente's Technical Computer Science asks for "mathematics comparable to a pre-university level, such as VWO Wiskunde B" and names no IB course or level. That is a requirement on a local scale — and it still does not make a case for a Recognition Scheme, because a scheme needs a published equivalence and nobody publishes one: not Twente, not Nuffic. A scheme here could only be invented, and the invention would sit between the university's sentence and the student's transcript, which is the thing ADR 0002 exists to prevent. So the requirement is recorded as kind 'other' with Twente's wording kept whole, and the engine tells the student it cannot check it and sends them to the official page. That Opportunity is the one of the sixteen that assesses as Needs review, and it should be.

The VWO comparison is used here only at qualification level — to establish that a full IB Diploma is required for a research university and that DP Course Results are not enough. It is never used to translate a subject or a grade, because no table exists that would allow it.

A finding worth its own line, because it is the one that would have been destroyed by a convenience: the two IB mathematics courses must be recorded separately and by name. TU Delft accepts only Analysis and Approaches HL and refuses Applications and Interpretation outright. Maastricht accepts Applications and Interpretation at SL for International Business, demands it at HL for Business Analytics and Econometrics, and refuses it entirely for Data Science and Computer Science — one university, one table, three answers. A 'mathematics' family shorthand would have told an Applications and Interpretation student they qualified for all of them.

MODEL FRICTION, all of it in src/ and none of it worked around in the data. (1) src/lib/canonical.mjs denormalise() understands only kind 'local-equivalency', so a requirement written in IB terms projects to entryRequirements: null and a Dutch programme page renders the heading 'And one of these combinations' above an empty list. ADR 0002 added the ib-subject path to the schema and to the engine; this projection into the page templates was not updated with it. (2) The same projection builds extraRequirements from the requirement kinds essay/test/portfolio/interview/audition/other without consulting `mandatory`, so a Selection Factor renders on the programme page under 'On top of the subjects' as though it were an entry requirement. On the Erasmus IBA page a student sees 'Your grade average — 75 per cent of the selection score' in the same list as things they must hold. The answer to 'can a student tell a Requirement from a Selection Factor on the page' is currently no. (3) assess() returns selection.factors and nothing renders it; admission.capacityNote is not rendered anywhere, so numerus fixus capacity and the hard 15 January date reach a page only through an Application Route milestone. (4) The restricted-admission note on a programme page is Danish copy — it talks about quota cut-offs and national intake policy — and it now appears on Dutch pages. (5) src/pages/programmes.mjs describes the planner as checking 'every English-taught programme in Denmark' and converting subjects 'using the Danish Agency's official table'; it now also checks sixteen Dutch ones and converts nothing for them.

MODEL FRICTION in the schema, found mechanically by the validator. A Requirement's `kind` enum and admission.selection[].type are two different vocabularies and neither contains the other. 'gpa', 'subject-grades', 'lottery' and 'work-experience' are selection types and are not requirement kinds — which means the four commonest Dutch ranking criteria cannot be named on the Requirement that carries them. They are recorded as kind 'other' or 'activity' with the precise mechanism in admission.selection and a note on each saying why.

MODEL FRICTION with no clean answer: a step that is compulsory and unweighted. The Dutch matching procedure (studiekeuzecheck) is exactly this, and so are TU Delft's Matching phase, Erasmus School of Economics' pass/fail curriculum activity and Twente's mandatory questionnaire and matching event. mandatory: true makes the engine answer 'needs review' for every student on a question that is not about eligibility; mandatory: false says it ranks them, which the sources explicitly deny — TU Delft: "they do not influence your place in the ranking". Recorded in admission.selection with weight 'none' plus a meta note, which is the least wrong shape available.

A near-miss between Requirement and Selection Factor that the model handles well and is worth keeping as the worked example: Rotterdam School of Management awards selection points only from 33 IB points upwards. Below 33 an applicant is still eligible and their application still stands; they simply score nothing and are therefore not in the running. Recorded as a Selection Factor with minPoints 33. Recorded as a Requirement it would tell a 32-point student they cannot apply, which is false.

A build check in src/lib/data.mjs treats every canonical institution as Danish and compares its id against the image keys derived from countries/nl.json. Canonical ids nl-um, nl-eur and nl-buas collided with the country profile's own entries for the same three universities and failed the build with 'one of them would show the other's photograph' — a false positive, since they are the same institutions. Since data/countries/nl.json was out of scope, the canonical ids were renamed to nl-maastricht, nl-erasmus and nl-breda-uas instead. The check is still wrong and will catch the next Destination that migrates.

What works end to end, checked rather than assumed: all sixteen Dutch Opportunities are assessed in /planner/ against a Danish IB profile — thirteen meet, Nanobiology is Possible with action for want of Biology HL, Technical Computer Science is Needs review for the reason above. The engine's sentence reads 'Your Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL meets HL. This requirement is published in IB terms, so nothing is converted.' That is ADR 0002 working as designed on a Destination with no Recognition Scheme, which is the test the ADR said had to pass.

Coverage as at 2026-09-23: 5 institutions, 16 Programmes, 16 Opportunities. Research universities TU Delft, Erasmus Rotterdam, Maastricht and Twente (universiteit); Breda University of Applied Sciences (hogeschool); University College Maastricht covers the university college route. The kunstacademie / conservatorium route is still unresearched and is recorded as such in sectorLandscape.

Not established across the pass: how any Dutch institution handles a conditional offer pending IB results published on about 6 July, except at Maastricht, where the certified diploma is an enrolment task due 31 August rather than an admission task. Capacity figures for TU Delft Nanobiology, all four Breda programmes and Maastricht International Business. Whether Breda's selection runs under the numerus fixus article of the WHW at all, which is why its 1 May deadline differs from the national 15 January.
